Sidon, Acco, and Old Tyre, on the mainland, were soon reduced; but New Tyre, on an island half a mile from the shore, held out for five years. Sargon probably finished the siege. Sennacherib does not, however, mention it among the cities which the Assyrian kings conquered (thirty-sixth and thirty-seventh chapters). The expression, "Chaldeans" (<reference osisRef="Isa.23.13">Is 23:13</reference>), may imply reference to its siege under Nebuchadnezzar, which lasted thirteen years. V. Smith]. Or, Tyre is so laid waste, that there is no possibility of entering the harbor [Barnes]; which is appropriate to the previous "ships."<div eID="gen14431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14432" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Chittim--</hi>Cyprus, of which the cities, including Citium in the south (whence came "Chittim"), were mostly Phoenician (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.6">Eze 27:6</reference>). entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 23 Is 23:1-18 . Prophecy Respecting Tyre. Menander, the historian, notices a siege of Tyre by Shalmaneser, about the time of the siege of Samaria. Sidon, Acco, and Old Tyre, on the mainland, were soon reduced; but New Tyre, on an island half a mile from the shore, held out for five years. Sargon probably finished the siege. Sennacherib does not, however, mention it among the cities which the Assyrian kings conquered (thirty-sixth and thirty-seventh chapters). The expression, "Chaldeans" ( Is 23:13 ), may imply reference to its siege under Nebuchadnezzar, which lasted thirteen years. Alexander the Great destroyed New Tyre after a seven months' siege. 1. Tyre-- Hebrew, Tsur, that is, "Rock." ships of Tarshish-- ships of Tyre returning from their voyage to Tarshish, or Tartessus in Spain, with which the Phoenicians had much commerce ( Eze 27:12-25 ). "Ships of Tarshish" is a phrase also used of large and distant-voyaging merchant vessels ( Is 2:16 ; 1Ki 10:22 ; Psa 48:7 ). no house-- namely, left; such was the case as to Old Tyre, after Nebuchadnezzar's siege. no entering-- There is no house to enter ( Is 24:10 ) [G. V. Smith]. Or, Tyre is so laid waste, that there is no possibility of entering the harbor [Barnes]; which is appropriate to the previous "ships." Chittim-- Cyprus, of which the cities, including Citium in the south (whence came "Chittim"), were mostly Phoenician ( Eze 27:6 ). The ships from Tarshish on their way to Tyre learn the tidings ("it is revealed to them") of the downfall of Tyre. At a later period Chittim denoted the islands and coasts of the Mediterranean ( Da 11:30 ).

Be still--</hi>"struck dumb with awe." Addressed to those already in the country, eye-witnesses of its ruin (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.10">La 2:10</reference>); or, in contrast to the busy din of commerce once heard in Tyre; now all is hushed and still.<div eID="gen14433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14434" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">isle--</hi>strictly applicable to New Tyre: in the sense coast, to the mainland city, Old Tyre (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.23.6">Is 23:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.20.6">Is 20:6</reference>).<div eID="gen14434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14435" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Zidon--</hi>of which Tyre was a colony, planted when Zidon was conquered by the Philistines of Ascalon. Zidon means a "fishing station"; this was its beginning.<div eID="gen14435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14436" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">replenished--</hi>with wealth and an industrious population (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.3">Eze 27:3</reference>, 8, 23). Here "Zidon," as the oldest city of Phoenicia, includes all the Phoenician towns on the strip of "coast." <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8731"/><div sID="gen14471" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8731"/><hi type="bold">15. forgotten--</hi>Having lost its former renown, Tyre shall be in obscurity.<div eID="gen14471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14472" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seventy years--</hi>(so <reference osisRef="Jer.25.11">Jr 25:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.29.10">29:10</reference>).<div eID="gen14472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14473" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">days of one king--</hi>that is, a dynasty. The Babylonian monarchy lasted properly but seventy years. From the first year of Nebuchadnezzar to the taking of Babylon, by Cyrus, was seventy years; then the subjected nations would be restored to liberty. Tyre was taken in the middle of that period, but it is classed in common with the rest, some conquered sooner and others later, all, however, alike to be delivered at the end of the period. So "king" is used for dynasty (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.17">Da 7:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.8.20">8:20</reference>): Nebuchadnezzar, his son Evil-merodach, and his grandson, Belshazzar, formed the whole dynasty (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.11">Jr 25:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.27.7">27:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.29.10">29:10</reference>).<div eID="gen14473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14474" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall Tyre sing as ... harlot--</hi>It shall be to Tyre as the song of the harlot, namely, a harlot that has been forgotten, but who attracts notice again by her song. Large marts of commerce are often compared to harlots seeking many lovers, that is, they court merchants of all nations, and admit any one for the sake of gain (<reference osisRef="Nah.3.4">Na 3:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.18.3">Re 18:3</reference>). Covetousness is closely akin to idolatry and licentiousness, as the connection (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.5">Ep 5:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.5">Col 3:5</reference>) proves (compare Is 2:6-8, 16). <div eID="gen14474" type="x-p"/>

navigation_sections.title: CHAPTER 23
navigation_sections.content_plain: CHAPTER 23 Is 23:1-18 . Prophecy Respecting Tyre. Menander, the historian, notices a siege of Tyre by Shalmaneser, about the time of the siege of Samaria. Sidon, Acco, and Old Tyre, on the mainland, were soon reduced; but New Tyre, on an island half a mile from the shore, held out for five years. Sargon probably finished the siege. Sennacherib does not, however, mention it among the cities which the Assyrian kings conquered (thirty-sixth and thirty-seventh chapters). The expression, "Chaldeans" ( Is 23:13 ), may imply reference to its siege under Nebuchadnezzar, which lasted thirteen years. Alexander the Great destroyed New Tyre after a seven months' siege.
